title: SLO drift investigation: node preemption + GPU warmup (customer escalations)
content:
SUMMARY

This document captures the investigation into an SLO drift observed by ExampleCorp (steady token generation workload) between 2025-10-14 and 2025-10-17. The symptoms were recurrent p95/p99 latency spikes correlating with scheduled cluster activity and autoscaler-driven node preemptions. Customer SLA impact: intermittent >30% increase in p99 generation latency for requests routed to affected nodes. The preliminary hotfix (scheduler change + GPU warmup preloader) was deployed as a canary on 2025-10-20 and validated before a phased rollout.

IMPACT
- Affected customer: ExampleCorp (production, dedicated pool, steady 200 requests/min, avg seq length 1.2k tokens).
- Observable metrics: p95 generation latency increased from baseline ~420ms to bursts up to ~1.8–2.4s when requests hit recently recreated worker pods. p99 reached 3.6s in the worst windows.
- Duration: recurring over 4 calendar days, worst around cluster autoscaler events at ~03:00 UTC when preemptible spot reclaim/checkpointing occurred.
- Business impact: several user-facing timeouts and two customer escalations to SEs + CSM.

DETECTION / SIGNALS
- Customer reported via support ticket and Slack escalation.
- Alerting: an internal SLO breach alert triggered on 2025-10-15 (automated detection of p99 > 2x baseline for 10m).
- Observability traces showed stack-level skew: requests routed to nodes with recent pod creation had noticeably higher time in "runtime:gpu-init" and "runtime:kv-repopulate" spans.

TIMELINE (abridged)
- 2025-10-14 22:40 UTC: ExampleCorp CS contacts support with intermittent latency reports.
- 2025-10-15 01:02 UTC: Platform SLO monitor fires p99 breach alert.
- 2025-10-15 03:10 UTC: Cluster autoscaler event—3 preemptible nodes reclaimed in us-west-2a, pods rescheduled into mixed instance pools.
- 2025-10-15 03:14 UTC: Traces show first post-reschedule requests incurring 1.2–3.6s extra latency.
- 2025-10-15 to 2025-10-17: Repeated patterns with small variance tied to node churn and scaledown/up cycles.
- 2025-10-18: Investigation kickoff meeting; capture of profiling artifacts.
- 2025-10-19: Root cause hypothesis formed: combined effect of GPU context reinitialization latency + KV cache repopulation + scheduler not preferring warm nodes.
- 2025-10-20: Hotfix PR #1782 opened and deployed to canary subset (10% of customer traffic in dedicated pool).
- 2025-10-21: Canary metrics show p99 reduction to ~700–900ms on canary nodes; rollout plan approved.

ROOT CAUSE ANALYSIS
We performed distributed tracing, flamegraphs from nanoprofile captures, and kernel-level profiling from the on-node agent. The major contributors were:

1) GPU context and library warmup (~600–1,400ms on cold pods)
- Observed: when a worker pod is started on a freshly-provisioned instance or after driver restart, CUDA/cuDNN/JIT compilation paths executed on first few inferences. The first token generation after pod start often triggered JIT load/compilation on our TF/XLA-dependent nightly builds (models with fused kernels). Measured median GPU init overhead: 860ms (sampled across 42 cold starts), 95th: 1,320ms.
- Root cause: lack of a systematic pre-warm path that triggers kernel loads on pod startup. Also, autoscaler pressured instance types with ephemeral images causing driver compatibility checks.

2) KV cache repopulation & prefix retrieval (~80–600ms variable)
- Observed: for chat session workloads, KV cache on new workers was cold; requests that relied on cached past tokens incurred extra decode work as cache warmed. The runtime's synchronous KV fetch path blocked request processing until first decoded chunks were available. Measured median KV warm cost per session start: 210ms; p95: 520ms.
- Root cause: synchronous blocking of request dispatch for KV repopulation and no prioritized async prefetch for sessions pinned to a pod.

3) Scheduler binpack decisions exposing cold pods (~120–500ms additional queueing)
- Observed: our scheduler (binpack) sometimes placed new pods on nodes with lower GPU occupancy, but it did not account for pod age or warm status. During autoscaler activity new pods were routed immediately into traffic. Measured added queueing/latency due to resource contention on new pods: median 180ms, p95 460ms.
- Root cause: scheduler policy lacked a "warmth" signal; node selection prioritized capacity rather than active warmed contexts.

Composite effect
- Cumulative cold-start path for some requests was: GPU init 860ms + KV repop 210ms + scheduler queueing 180ms = ~1.25s median additional latency, with upper tail exceeding 3s when multiple slow factors compounded. This aligns with the p99 observed.

CUSTOMER ESCALATION HANDLING
- Triage: SEs collected customer traces and shared with infra team. We coordinated a live debugging window with ExampleCorp on 2025-10-16 to correlate request IDs.
- Communication: regular updates posted to the support ticket and a joint call on 2025-10-17. We committed to a mitigations timeline and provided a temporary workaround (increase request timeout and route traffic to pre-warmed canary nodes).

SHORT-TERM MITIGATIONS (implemented)
1) Scheduler tweak (hotfix PR #1782) — immediate: 2025-10-20
- Change: prefer nodes with last-pod-age > 15m or with "warm" annotation; during scale-up avoid immediate routing of production traffic to pods younger than 60s unless they pass a warmup probe.
- Rationale: reduce exposure of live traffic to freshly-created, cold pods.

2) GPU warmup preloader — immediate canary: 2025-10-20
- Change: on pod start, async warmup worker executes a small number of token-generation iterations using a tiny synthetic prompt to force kernel loads and JIT paths. This runs before the pod marks itself "serving-healthy".
- Overhead: adds ~120ms to pod readiness in exchange for cutting per-request cold penalty.

3) Async KV prefetch for session-aware routes — canary: 2025-10-21
- Change: when a session is scheduled to a pod, background prefetch of KV prefix begins using session metadata (if available) so first real request does not block on fetch.

CANARY VALIDATION RESULTS
- Canary cohort: 10% traffic from ExampleCorp (dedicated pool), 5 canary pods across two nodes. Measurement window: 24h after deployment.
- Key results vs baseline (non-canary traffic during same interval):
  - p50 latency: unchanged (~360–430ms)
  - p95 latency: improved from 820ms -> 420ms on canary nodes (stable)
  - p99 latency: improved from 1.9s -> 0.78s on canary nodes (observed across sample of 18 cold-start events)
  - Rate of requests that observed >1s extra cold penalty: reduced by 87% in canary cohort.
- Observability: traces show the gpu-init span collapsed from median 860ms to median ~110ms (because warmup did heavy lifting) and KV warmspan moved from median 210ms to ~60ms thanks to prefetch.
- Costs: marginal increase in pod readiness time and minor additional vCPU cycles on pod init. No measurable increase in steady-state GPU utilization.

RISKS AND TRADE-OFFS
- Warmer-first scheduling increases likelihood of under-utilization for short-lived batch loads, possibly raising per-token cost.
- Warmup preloader increases pod readiness latency and slightly raises startup CPU/GPU cycles. For extremely elastic, short-lived workloads this could be suboptimal.
- Async prefetch requires careful memory management to avoid thrashing KV store for very large session histories.

LONGER-TERM ACTIONS (owners + ETA)
1) Persistent per-node warm pools (owner: Priya Nair, ETA: 2026-01-15)
- Keep a small pool of pre-warmed pods per node/class to absorb scale events without cold-starting user traffic.

2) Scheduler "warmth" metric and API (owner: Liam O'Connor, ETA: 2025-12-10)
- Expose a pod/node warmth score, integrate into binpack decision and autoscaler heuristics.

3) Lazy JIT snapshotting & model kernel caching (owner: Diego Morales, ETA: 2026-02-28)
- Persist compiled kernels per model build and reuse across pod lifetimes; investigate kernel cache hot-reload to cut first-time JIT costs.

4) KV prefetch prioritization & memory caps (owner: Katrina Wu, ETA: 2025-12-20)
- Smarter heuristics for which sessions to prefetch and evict policy to keep memory bounded.

5) Expand test harness to include spot/preempt scenarios (owner: Maya Chen, ETA: 2025-11-30)
- Add automated chaos tests that simulate node preemption and measure tail latency to prevent regression.

POST-ROLLOUT OBSERVATIONS
- After full rollout on 2025-10-24, ExampleCorp reported significant reduction in perceived timeouts and closed the escalation ticket. Platform SLOs stabilized back below alert thresholds.
- No new regressions observed in next two weeks; continuous monitoring planned.

LESSONS LEARNED
- Cold-starts for GPU-backed serving are multidimensional: kernel/JIT startup, KV state, and scheduler decisions combine non-linearly. Fixing any single dimension reduces impact but multiple coordinated mitigations yield robust tail-latency improvements.
- Observability must track "pod age" in traces and metrics so we can quickly correlate bursts with pod churn events.
- Canarying and small warm pools are effective for dedicated customer clusters where tight SLOs are required.

APPENDIX: ARTIFACTS & REPRO STEPS
1) Reproduce locally (dev cluster):
- Launch a small cluster with preemptible nodes and identical AMI/driver stack from prod image.
- Start serving runtime with debug logging on GPU init and KV fetch: set LOG_LEVEL=debug and PROFILING_SAMPLING=1
- Simulate customer load using loadgen: steady 200 req/min, seq len 1.2k tokens, session reuse pattern.
- Trigger scale-down events via cluster autoscaler or delete nodes to force pod reschedule.
- Observe traces for spans: runtime:gpu-init, runtime:kv-repopulate, runtime:queue-delay.

2) Useful queries (observability)
- Trace search: tag:customer:ExampleCorp AND span:runtime:gpu-init AND timestamp:[2025-10-15 TO 2025-10-16]
- Metrics: sum(rate(requests_total{pool="examplecorp-dedicated"}[1m])) by (pod) vs histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))

3) Related PRs & tickets
- SRV-2143: investigate SLO tail regressions during autoscaler activity
- PR #1782: scheduler tweak + warmup preloader

If anything in this doc is unclear or you want the raw profiling captures (flamegraphs and per-kernel timelines), I have uploads stored under the incident artifacts bucket and can attach them or link them into the Confluence doc.

Owner sign-off: Maya Chen (eng-serving-runtime)
